page_one:
A readiness diagnostic of federal statistical websites
Brief for the working group, 16 October 2026
Why
No new burden. The diagnostic uses what agencies already publish on their public websites. It needs no survey, no data call 
and no agency staff time.
The public data user is the customer. A machine is now one of the main ways members of the public reach federal data, so the 
diagnostic takes the machine's view as the public's proxy, to show what their experience is and how it could improve.
Anyone can do this. Any member of the public with a laptop can make the same requests. The diagnostic writes the questions 
and the method down, so the answer does not depend on who asks.
Who
The public client identifies itself by one fixed name in every request, so a site's own logs show each request it made: ai-
readiness-kg-scanner/0.2 (+https://github.com/brockwebb/ai-readiness-kg)
The name still carries the project's earlier word for the client; it is kept unchanged so that one log search finds every request.
It makes no more than 1 request per second to any one website, and waits longer when a site asks it to.
What the public client never does
 No sign-in or password.
 No form filled in.
 No challenge or CAPTCHA solved, and no block worked around.
 No page scripts run.
 Nothing taken beyond what the page itself serves.
Not measured means the client could not look, and the footnote says why. It is never counted as a fail.
The checks
The diagnostic runs 16 checks. 4 are scored; the rest are shown so the method is open, and produce no finding about an 
agency.
Check What we ask your site for What it tells us Why it matters

A W3C practice asks for interface

What robots.txt lets answer-

Declaration
The site's robots.txt file, which 
search engines also request as a 
matter of course.
Whether the site's written policy 
lets the crawlers behind answer 
engines reach the data page.
An OMB memo asks agencies to 
use robots.txt; treating certain

rule.
The page labels itself as a dataset
Shown, not scored
The data page itself, reading the 
descriptive labels built into its 
code for search engines.
Whether a search or answer 
engine can recognise the page as 
a named, described dataset.
The schema.org dataset 
vocabulary defines these labels, 
and USAFacts' guide asks for 
standard metadata.
The release date, and a link to 
the latest release
Shown, not scored
Date labels in the data page's 
code, and up to three links that 
point to the latest version.
Whether a program can tell which 
release it is reading and find a 
newer one.
A W3C practice asks that a 
dataset's version be detectable; 
requiring the link to work is this 
project's rule.

objections.passage: No new burden. The diagnostic uses what agencies already publish on their public websites. It needs no survey, no data call and no agency staff time.
objections.objection: Wrong on its face. My staff will spend time reading this brief, reviewing our logs, answering the inevitable questions from leadership, and responding to whatever gets published about us. 'No new burden' is a claim about the data collection, but the reputational and workload burden of being publicly scored is real, and you chose not to ask us.

I was never asked. You are scoring my agency by name without notice, consent, or a chance to review the method or findings before a working group sees them. Public availability of a website does not make public ranking of it benign.

objections.passage: The public data user is the customer. A machine is now one of the main ways members of the public reach federal data, so the diagnostic takes the machine's view as the public's proxy
objections.objection: Unsupported empirical claim, stated as fact with no citation or measurement. Our own traffic data would have to show it. And a scanner is not a member of the public: calling the machine a 'proxy' for the public's experience is a leap that quietly justifies the whole design. Also 'customer' is not how a statistical agency frames its relationship to the public.

objections.passage: Anyone can do this. Any member of the public with a laptop can make the same requests.
objections.objection: Reproducible in principle is not the same as equivalent. A laptop user is not a fixed-identity scanner hitting every statistical agency on a schedule. This reads as pre-empting a complaint about the scanning rather than answering it. The reproducibility point is fine; using it as moral cover is not.

objections.passage: The public client identifies itself by one fixed name in every request, so a site's own logs show each request it made: ai-readiness-kg-scanner/0.2 (+https://github.com/brockwebb/ai-readiness-kg)
objections.objection: Identifying itself is good, but the name says 'ai-readiness-kg-scanner', i.e. an AI readiness scoring project, which is not what the page calls it ('diagnostic', 'public client'). The page softens what the thing is. Also, a user-agent my bot rules may block, and the page does not say what happens to my scores if I block it.

objections.passage: The name still carries the project's earlier word for the client; it is kept unchanged so that one log search finds every request.
objections.objection: This admits the name is a different word from the one used here, and does not say what the earlier word was. It reads as an admission that the framing was changed for this audience. It also invites the question of what else was renamed.

objections.passage: It makes no more than 1 request per second to any one website, and waits longer when a site asks it to.
objections.objection: 'When a site asks it to' is vague. Does it honor Crawl-delay, Retry-After, 429s, robots.txt disallow for its own user agent? The page lists what it never does but never says it obeys robots.txt, which is conspicuous given that one of the checks is about robots.txt policy. One request per second for a full crawl can still be material on a small or shared host.

objections.passage: Nothing taken beyond what the page itself serves.
objections.objection: Ambiguous. It does not say whether pages and files are stored, retained, redistributed or fed to a model, or for how long. 'Taken' is a worrying word to use for a retrieval.

objections.passage: Not measured means the client could not look, and the footnote says why. It is never counted as a fail.
objections.objection: Where a block, CAPTCHA, or timeout stops the scanner, I need to know that is never read as 'not ready'. Also the claim is stated but there is no evidence here, and the footnote is not on page one. A bot-protected site silently dropping out of the denominator is itself a bias.

objections.passage: 4 are scored; the rest are shown so the method is open, and produce no finding about an agency.
objections.objection: 16 checks run but only 4 scored, and only 7 are visible on this page. 'Shown, not scored' items will still appear next to my agency's name and will be read as findings by journalists and Congress regardless of the label. 'Open method' is also the justification for displaying results I have not seen.

objections.passage: The data page is in the site's sitemap | Scored
objections.objection: Penalizes agencies for not doing something that is a search-engine optimisation convention, not a requirement for being accessible. A statistical site that has chosen not to list pages in a sitemap is not less accessible to a person. Also, how is 'the data page' identified for my agency? Who chose it? If the scanner picks the wrong page I get scored for it.

objections.passage: The whole dataset in one download | Scored
objections.objection: Many of our datasets cannot be released as a single file for disclosure-avoidance, size, or confidentiality (Title 13, CIPSEA, Title 26) reasons, and query-based access is a deliberate design. Scoring bulk download as a plus penalizes legitimate confidentiality protection. Citing an OMB memo for 'bulk access' does not make absence a failure.

objections.passage: An OMB memo requires public data to be machine-readable, and USAFacts' guide says to avoid PDF-only release.
objections.objection: Which OMB memo, which number, which paragraph? 'An OMB memo' appears four times with no citation. An advocacy or third-party guide (USAFacts) is cited as if it carried authority comparable to a mandate. I cannot verify any of it from this page.

objections.passage: the required file format is this project's rule. / treating certain blocks as failures is this project's rule. / requiring the link to work is this project's rule.
objections.objection: Honest, but it concedes that several criteria are the project's own invention rather than any standard. Then the scores are the authors' preferences presented alongside OMB and W3C authority. Who gave this project the standing to set rules and rank federal agencies?

objections.passage: What robots.txt lets answer-engine crawlers fetch | Declaration
objections.objection: Treating a robots.txt block of AI crawlers as a failure penalizes an agency for exercising a legitimate policy choice about how its content is used. 'Declaration' is a third label that is not explained. The check also leans on a particular commercial industry's interests.

objections.passage: Brief for the working group, 16 October 2026
objections.objection: I do not know who the working group is, who the authors are, who funds this, or what authority it has. The page names a GitHub repo but not an institution or a person accountable.

words_not_understood: descriptive labels built into its code
reading.secretly_doing: They're building a public league table that grades federal statistical agencies on how well AI tools can scrape and ingest their data, and dressing it up as a neutral, no-burden, 'public user' exercise. The real aim is to pressure us into restructuring our sites for AI consumption and bulk release, with the project's own preferences baked into the scoring, and with the AI angle softened ('public client' instead of AI scanner). The 'anyone could do this' and 'no burden' language is cover so we can't object to being scanned and scored without being asked.
